newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai finmin says to sustain monetary policies.
newsitem.headline: New Thai finmin says to sustain monetary policies.

text.p: New Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said on Friday he would pursue fiscal and monetary policies of his predecessor Amnuay Viravan saying they were mostly on the right track in tackling Thai economic problems.

Thanong said at his first press conference after his appointment that he would seek additional measures from those adopted by Amnuay to shore up the Thai economy which has slowed to its most sluggish level in 10 years.

Private economists projected that the Thai gross domestic product would expand three to five percent this year against 6.4 percent in 1996 and nearly 10 percent annual growth in the first half of this decade.

"Our national problems have gradually built up to the extent that, many feel, still have not been resolved...Amnuay has adopted appropriate measures in line with international practices, measures dealing with fiscal and monetary problems which I believe are on the right track and if there is anything that I could do to continue the job, I would definitely do so."
Thanong, a low profile banker and chief executive of Thai Military Bank Plc, succeeded respected fellow banker Amnuay who quit on Thursday after less than seven months in the job.

Amnuay's resignation triggered renewed speculation that Thailand may change its foreign exchange regime by either devalueing its baht or easing a current small spread that the baht was allowed to fluctuate against other currencies.
The new finance minister declined to commit himself to any change in the baht policy or comment on high Thai interest rates which the government maintained to discourage capital outflows.
Thai prime lending rates, at 12.75-13.50 percent, are among the highest in the region. Analysts and businessmen have blamed the rates for stifling economic recovery.

The minister also failed to spell out what he planned to do for rescueing Thailand's battered finance companies which faced a crisis of confidence and acute liquidity problems arising from their over-exposure to the property sector. He said only that he would continue working with the central bank in encouraging finance companies to consolidate through mergers.
The minister said he would consult the Bank of Thailand and senior finance ministry officials before announcing his policy in the next few days.
Thanong's predecessor quit after differences with political rivals in the six-party coalition government of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh.

Asked if he expected to face the same political problem as Amnuay, the new minister said Chavalit did not interfere with works of his ministers and his appointment to the finance portfolio was a concensus decision of political party leaders in Chavalit's coalition.

"(Chavalit) knows that I like to have independence in my work but the word independence does not mean working alone... I don't believe we have time to squabble as that would only aggravate national problems...we need to jointly set national priorities and agenda," he said.
Thanong declined to set a time-frame for turning around the economy but said he was confident that he could handle the job.

"I would not be sitting here if I don't believe I can do it. The issue is not how long I would need to do the job. The important thing is I must start doing it now and do my best... Time and the media would judge my performance," he said.

Thanong said his banking experience and past economic research works at the World Bank would help him clarify to foreign investors about Thailand's situation which he said was not unique or beyond solutions. REUTER VA
